headline: Delta just showed what $4.25 jet fuel costs, OpenAI's smaller revenue number knocked the AI infrastructure trade, and the bond market took the 30-year auction in stride; stay patient with entries until Hurricane Isaias lands tonight.
summary: Stocks split on Thursday: the Nasdaq fell 1.25% to 27,193.34, its worst day since mid August, after OpenAI put its annualized revenue near $50 billion instead of the roughly $68 billion reported in September, while the Dow edged up 0.10%. The $22 billion 30-year auction cleared at 5.618% with ordinary demand (bid-to-cover 2.54), and long yields then fell about 7 basis points, so the auction scare is behind us for now. Jobless claims fell to 197,000, so the job market is not cracking. This morning Delta cut its 2026 profit outlook to $5.10 to $5.60 a share and now assumes about $4.25 a gallon for fourth quarter fuel. Oil eased (Brent about $103) after President Trump said there would be no strike on Iran before the Nov 3 midterms, but Isaias strengthened to a Category 3 and is due to land tonight east of Mobile with nearly two thirds of Gulf oil output shut in. Her MT Swing Setup scan found zero names on Oct 8 while the dashboard still lists seven setups; none has reached its entry price yet, so nothing needs doing until price confirms.

regime.why: Breadth of the selloff was narrow: tech fell on an AI revenue scare while the Dow rose, VIX sits near 15, and futures are up this morning. But the 10-year is still about 5.2%, oil is above $100, the Fed says one more hike is likely, and the AI trade just got its first real demand question. Hold leaders with stops, add only on confirmed breakouts, keep size normal.

signals.title: Delta confirms the fuel shock: guidance cut, $4.25 jet fuel assumed, and the storm hits tonight
signals.what_happened: Delta reported third quarter adjusted EPS of $1.72, just under the $1.76 estimate, and cut its 2026 outlook to $5.10 to $5.60 a share from $6.50 to $7.50 in July. Adjusted fuel cost rose 62% to $4.14 billion, more than $500 million above its July plan. It guides fourth quarter EPS of $1.15 to $1.65 (estimate $1.51) and assumes about $4.25 a gallon, up from $3.61 in the third quarter. Free cash flow guidance fell to $2.5 billion. CEO Ed Bastian says demand is still strong and fares keep rising. Meanwhile Isaias became a Category 3 and is expected to land between Dauphin Island, Alabama and Destin, Florida between 8pm and 1am EDT; nearly two thirds of Gulf oil output and 57% of gas output were shut in by noon Thursday.
signals.so_what: Who pays: airlines and anyone buying diesel or jet fuel, and in the end travelers through higher fares. Who gets paid: refiners, because jet and diesel are the tight products. Delta's own refinery is expected to earn about $700 million this year, which shows how much margin sits in refining right now. Second order: Delta can pass on part of the cost because demand is firm, which is good for Delta versus weaker airlines but feeds inflation and keeps the Fed alert before the Oct 14 CPI. Third order: if Isaias floods Pascagoula or Mobile area plants, product prices jump again; if the track keeps moving east toward Pensacola, refiners in Texas and Louisiana are spared and still get the price. Honest note: refiners have run a lot already and her MT Breakout Trigger flagged VLO and MPC on Oct 8, so a lot of good news is priced. What would make this wrong: Hormuz traffic recovers after the Iran pledge, or the storm weakens before landfall.

signals.title: OpenAI's $50 billion run rate is the first real demand question for the AI build, and CoreWeave broke its line
signals.what_happened: On Oct 8 OpenAI told investors its annualized revenue was about $50 billion at the end of September, below the roughly $68 billion figure that circulated in late September. Reports say the gap is mostly a counting difference (the higher number included partner revenue), and OpenAI said run rate growth was 77% in the quarter. Oracle fell nearly 6%, CoreWeave nearly 8%, Nvidia 3%, AMD and Broadcom 4%. CoreWeave closed at 81.58, under the dashboard thesis break of about 83.34.
signals.so_what: Who pays for the AI build: a short list of buyers, and OpenAI is the biggest single customer for Oracle and a key one for CoreWeave. If its revenue is smaller, the debt funded data center plans tied to it carry more risk. That hits the names that borrowed to build (ORCL, CRWV) harder than the chip and memory suppliers, whose order books are spread across many buyers and were just confirmed by TSMC and Samsung. Second order: CoreWeave can start selling shares under its 35 million share at the market program from about mid October, which adds supply into weakness. Third order: Microsoft, which holds a large OpenAI stake, also earns on Azure from many customers, so it is hurt less than the neoclouds. Honest note: 77% growth on $50 billion is still huge; this is a valuation reset, not a collapse. What would make this wrong: OpenAI shows the larger gross number is real revenue, or hyperscalers raise 2027 capex in late October.

signals.title: SpaceX buys nationwide low band spectrum, and the big phone carriers drop 5% to 7%
signals.what_happened: On Oct 8 SpaceX agreed to buy Grain Management's nationwide 800 MHz low band licenses, which Grain bought from T-Mobile in August. The Wall Street Journal put the price near $8 billion in cash; FCC approval is still needed. By the close of after hours trading AT&T was down 7.3% and Verizon and T-Mobile 6.6%; premarket Friday T-Mobile was down 6.3%, AT&T 5.7% and Verizon 5.1%. The FCC separately approved a 15,000 satellite Starlink Mobile Gen2 constellation.
signals.so_what: Low band spectrum travels far and goes through walls, which was the missing piece for Starlink phone service. The scarce thing in wireless is licensed spectrum, and SpaceX now owns some. Who gets hurt first: rural phone service, where carriers earn the most per tower and coverage is thin. Morgan Stanley says the threat is real but rural first. Second order: carriers may need to spend more on rural networks or cut prices, which pressures the dividends that most people own these stocks for. Honest note: the dashboard rates T Buy zone now at 24.87, but that price is from before the after hours drop and the valuation model does not know about a new competitor, so treat that verdict with care. What would make this wrong: the FCC blocks or delays the transfer, or satellite phone service stays a niche product.

signals.title: The 30-year auction passed, claims stayed low, and Trump took an Iran strike off the table until the vote
signals.what_happened: Treasury sold $22 billion of 30-year bonds on Oct 8 at 5.618%, 31 basis points above the September sale and the highest since 2000, with a 2.54 bid-to-cover (recent average about 2.41) and indirect bidders taking 72.3%. The 30-year yield then fell 7 basis points to 5.60% and the 10-year closed at 5.22%. Initial jobless claims fell 2,000 to 197,000 for the week ended Oct 3, below the 200,000 expected and the fourth straight week under 200,000. President Trump said the US would not strike Iran before the Nov 3 midterms, and Brent eased to about $103 Friday morning after a 4% gain Thursday.
signals.so_what: Two auctions in a row found buyers above 5.3%, so the fear of a buyers' strike is fading and the bond story is now about inflation: oil and the Oct 14 CPI. A firm job market plus $100 oil gives the Fed room to hike on Oct 28 or in December, which keeps cash yields high (good for cash backing short puts) and keeps pressure on homebuilders and small caps. The Iran pledge removes one tail risk for a few weeks but not the tanker attacks: Hormuz flows were about 30% below normal last week per Kpler. What would make this wrong: a hot CPI, or a new Hormuz incident that sends Brent back above $105.

signals.title: Immunotherapy moves into stage III colon cancer: FDA approves Tecentriq after surgery for dMMR tumors
signals.what_happened: The FDA approved Roche's Tecentriq (atezolizumab) with FOLFOX chemotherapy as adjuvant treatment for resected stage III colon cancer with deficient mismatch repair (dMMR), announced Oct 9. It rests on the phase 3 ATOMIC trial (Alliance A021502, 712 patients): adding Tecentriq cut the risk of recurrence or death by 50%, with 3 year disease free survival of 86% versus 76% for mFOLFOX6 alone. It is the first immunotherapy regimen approved in this setting and Tecentriq's twelfth US indication. Eligibility uses an MMR immunohistochemistry test such as Roche's VENTANA MMR RxDx panel.
signals.so_what: For a clinician: this changes standard adjuvant care for a molecularly defined subset that until now got chemotherapy alone. Overall survival is not yet shown, and adding an immune drug adds immune side effects, so expect oncologists to weigh this case by case. Who gets paid: Roche twice, on the drug (infused, billed under Medicare Part B) and on the companion MMR test. Second order: universal MMR testing of colon tumors becomes more clearly required, a small tailwind for pathology labs and test makers. RHHBY sits in the dashboard buy zone (53.37, zone 51.21 to 55.86), but Tecentriq is one drug among many at Roche, so this is a quality add, not a stock mover. What would make this wrong: longer follow up shows no survival gain, or Merck's Keytruda wins a similar label and takes share.
